title: Glossary
markdown:
**Address**: the number of a byte in a program's memory. (1.01)

**Alignment**: the number an object's address must be a multiple of; usually its size for basic types. (3.01)

**Aliasing**: two pointers or references reaching the same object. (1.03)

**Arena**: an allocator that hands out memory by moving one offset forward and frees everything at once. (6.02)

**ASLR**: address space layout randomisation; Windows loads each part of a program at a random address every run. (1.01)

**Borrower**: code holding a pointer to an object it does not own and must not free. (4.04)

**Coalescing**: merging neighbouring free blocks into one. (6.01)

**Commit**: back a reserved range of addresses with real memory. (6.04)

**Control block**: the separate block holding a `shared_ptr`'s reference counts. (5.03)

**Dangling pointer**: a pointer to an object that no longer exists. (1.05)

**Decay**: an array's name turning into a pointer to its first element. (2.01)

**Dereference**: follow a pointer to the object at its address, with `*` or `->`. (1.03)

**Fragmentation**: free memory split into pieces too small to use. (6.01)

**Frame**: the part of the stack used by one function call: return address and locals. (4.02)

**Free list**: a linked list of free blocks, stored inside the blocks. (6.01, 6.03)

**Handle**: an index plus a generation number, used instead of a pointer so that stale references are detected. (1.05)

**Heap**: memory allocated at run time with `new` or `malloc`, alive until freed. (4.03)

**Little-endian**: storing the least significant byte of a number at the lowest address. (1.01)

**Offset**: the distance in bytes from the start of an object to one of its members. (3.01)

**Owner**: the one piece of code responsible for freeing an object. (4.04)

**Padding**: unused bytes the compiler inserts to keep members aligned. (3.01)

**Page**: the 4 KB unit in which virtual memory is mapped and protected. (6.04)

**Pointer chain**: a base address and a list of offsets, followed one pointer read at a time. (3.03)

**Pool**: an allocator for blocks of one fixed size. (6.03)

**RAII**: tying a resource to an object whose destructor releases it. (5.01)

**Reserve**: set aside a range of addresses without memory behind it. (6.04)

**Sentinel**: a dummy node that removes special cases from a linked structure. (3.04)

**Span**: a non-owning view of a sequence: a pointer and a length. (5.04)

**Stack**: per-thread memory used for function frames, growing downwards. (4.02)

**Stride**: the distance from the start of one row to the start of the next. (2.04)

**Strict aliasing**: the rule that an object may only be read through its own type or a char type. (2.05)

**Use after free**: reading or writing an object after it was deleted. (1.05)

**Virtual address**: an address as the program sees it, translated by the processor to a physical one. (6.04)

**Vtable**: a class's table of virtual function addresses. (3.05)

**Wild pointer**: a pointer that was never initialised. (1.05)
